description_full: Franklin Electric Co., Inc., together with its subsidiaries, designs, manufactures, and distributes water and fuel pumping systems in the United States, Canada, Latin America, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and the Asia Pacific. It operates through Water Systems, Energy Systems, and Distribution segments. The Water Systems segment offers motors, pumps, water treatment systems, monitoring devices, and related parts and equipment for use in groundwater, water transfer, and wastewater in a range of residential, agricultural, municipal, and industrial applications; and electronic drives and controls for the motors, which control functionality and provide protection from various hazards, such as electrical surges, over-heating, and dry wells or dry tanks. Its Energy Systems segment produces and markets pumps, motors, pipes, sumps, fittings, vapor recovery components, electronic controls, monitoring devices, and related parts and equipment for use in energy system applications; and components between the tanks and the dispensers, including submersible pumps, station hardware, piping, and corrosion control systems. This segment serves other energy markets, such as power reliability systems, including intelligent electronic devices that are designed for online monitoring for the power utility, hydroelectric, rail, and telecommunication and data center infrastructure. The Distribution segment sells to and provides presale support and specifications to the installing contractors. In addition, the company manufactures precision triplex reciprocating pumps and systems. It sells its products to wholesale and retail distributors, specialty distributors, and industrial and petroleum equipment distributors, as well as to oil and utility companies, and original equipment manufacturers. The company was founded in 1944 and is headquartered in Fort Wayne, Indiana.

financial_summary: Franklin Electric Co., Inc. is a mid-cap industrials business with a $4.2B market cap on $2.1B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +1% over the past three years and +9% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 16% against a 9% cost of capital, a 7-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 34%.

The business throws off $194M in free cash flow — roughly 9 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.62× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.2× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 25× is fortress-like.
Management returns a meaningful 5.1% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 7.3% of the shares.

growth: Revenue has compounded at 1.4% over 3 years, 11.3% over 5 years and 8.7% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.

Free cash flow has compounded 0.5% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs only 0.7x depreciation (2.1% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 20, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.

own: Insiders own 7.3%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 95%.
It returns 5.1% a year to shareholders (3.9% in buybacks and 1.2% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 1.0% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 33 consecutive years, raising it 11.0% a year over the last five.
people: With about 6,500 employees, each generates about $328K of revenue, in line with the Industrials median, and productivity has risen 7.6% a year.
That works out to $30K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.6M (5x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
